findings.title: Computed zod schema keys are invalid and will reject all responses when credential sync is enabled
findings.body: The schema uses computed keys `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()`. `z.string().toString()` does not produce a real property name (it stringifies the ZodString object, e.g. "[object Object]"), so the resulting schema requires a numeric property literally named e.g. "[object Object]" and a second garbage key. Any real OAuth token response (which has keys like `expires_in`, `expiry_date`) will fail `safeParse`, so whenever APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, every token refresh for Google, Office 365, Zoom and Salesforce will throw "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" and those integrations break. The intended behavior (accept any numeric expiry property and allow extra fields) needs `.passthrough()` and a union/optional expiry field, not computed keys.

findings.title: Placeholder refresh_token overwrites real refresh tokens in the database
findings.body: When the parsed response lacks a refresh_token (which is the normal case for the self-hoster sync endpoint that only returns access token and expiry), the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers (Zoom, Webex, Google, Office365, Zoho) then persist this parsed object as the credential key. The real refresh token is permanently replaced by the literal string "refresh_token", so the next refresh attempt (and any fallback that disables sync) will fail with invalid_grant and the credential becomes unrecoverable. The old refresh_token must be merged in by the caller before saving, not defaulted to a bogus placeholder.

findings.title: Sync endpoint response shape is incompatible with all callers
findings.body: When sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` Response of CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, but every call site was written against the original provider's response type: Google reads `res?.data` (undefined on a fetch Response, so `token.access_token`/`expiry_date` become undefined and undefined is persisted to the credential), Hubspot expects the SDK's camelCase `HubspotToken` object, Lark passes the response to `handleLarkError` which requires Lark's `{code:0, data:{...}}` envelope, and Office365-video/Zoom/Webex/Zoho pass it to handlers expecting axios `response.data`. There is no contract (documented or validated) for the sync endpoint's response body, and the code never parses it before use, so token refresh is broken or corrupts credentials for every integration when the feature is turned on.

findings.title: No HTTP method check and unhandled zod/JSON.parse errors cause 500s
findings.body: The handler runs for any HTTP method (GET, DELETE, etc.) and does not guard `req.method === "POST"`. Additionally `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throws on malformed ciphertext or non-JSON plaintext; neither is caught, so invalid requests produce unhandled 500 errors with stack traces instead of 400s. Wrap parsing in safeParse, return 400 on failure, and restrict the handler to POST.

findings.title: symmetricDecrypt called with empty-key fallback; unvalidated decrypted payload written to credential key
findings.body: `symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || "")` silently falls back to an empty key. If the env var is unset (e.g. only CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is configured), decryption either fails obscurely or, depending on symmetricDecrypt's behavior with an empty key, may succeed incorrectly. More importantly, the decrypted value is `JSON.parse`d and written directly as the credential `key` with no schema validation — any JSON of any shape is accepted and persisted, so a compromised/misbehaving sender can store arbitrary credential payloads that will later crash app services when they try to use them. Validate against the app's expected credential schema before persisting, and fail loudly if the encryption key is missing.

findings.title: Credential lookup ignores type and can overwrite team credentials
findings.body: `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` matches any credential for the user with that appId, including team-owned or differently-typed credentials (a user can legitimately have multiple credentials for the same app, e.g. google_calendar plus google_video share client ids across app slugs, and apps like office365 expose both calendar and video types). The webhook update will then overwrite whichever credential `findFirst` happens to return (no orderBy, so nondeterministic), potentially clobbering a team credential or the wrong app-type credential. Scope the lookup by `type: appMetadata.type` (and exclude team credentials) as done on create.

findings.title: credentialId passed to refreshOAuthTokens instead of userId
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes the credential's id where the function expects the user's id (`calcomUserId`). When credential sync is enabled, the self-hoster's endpoint receives the credential id as `calcomUserId`, so it cannot resolve the right user and the token refresh will fail or return the wrong user's tokens. All other call sites pass `credential.userId`; this should too.

findings.title: Refreshed Salesforce access token saved to DB but not used for the connection
findings.body: In `getClient`, the newly fetched token is validated and persisted via `prisma.credential.update`, but the returned `jsforce.Connection` is still constructed with the stale `credentialKey.access_token` (line 106). The first API call after refresh therefore uses the expired token and fails; the refreshed token only takes effect the next time the service is constructed. Use `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token` (and the refreshed instance_url) when building the connection.

findings.title: Response success checked via response.statusText instead of response.ok
findings.body: `if (response.statusText !== "OK")` relies on the human-readable reason phrase, which is not guaranteed to be "OK" for 200 responses across HTTP/2 (where reason phrases don't exist) or proxies. Use `response.ok` / `response.status === 200`, otherwise valid refreshes may be rejected or errors misclassified.

findings.title: Outbound token sync request is unauthenticated and has no timeout
findings.body: The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no authentication (no webhook secret or signature), so the receiving self-hoster endpoint cannot verify the request actually came from its Cal.com instance, and anyone who can reach the endpoint can request access tokens for arbitrary users. There is also no timeout or non-200 handling — a slow or failing endpoint will hang every booking that triggers a token refresh. Attach the CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET header and check the response status before returning.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED depends on CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT too, misleading gating
findings.body: The flag is true whenever CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET and CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY are set, even if CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is empty. In that configuration the webhook is enabled but every refresh call site takes the normal path (each also checks the endpoint separately), which is arguably intended — but `parseRefreshTokenResponse` switches to the broken `minimumTokenResponseSchema` based on both flag and endpoint while `refreshOAuthTokens` uses the same pair of conditions evaluated at different times, making the behavior inconsistent and hard to reason about. Consolidate the enablement condition (flag + endpoint) into one shared constant so webhook receipt and refresh-path behavior cannot diverge.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with strict equality (not timing-safe)
findings.body: The CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET header is compared using `!==`, which is not constant-time. Use a timing-safe comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual on digested values) for secret verification, as is standard for webhook endpoints, to avoid leaking the secret byte-by-byte to an attacker who can make repeated requests.

findings.title: Missing Content-Type header on the sync POST request
findings.body: The fetch to the credential sync endpoint sends a `URLSearchParams` body but no `Content-Type` header. While fetch infers `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` for URLSearchParams in modern runtimes, the endpoint contract is undocumented and some servers/parsers require the explicit header; a request that the receiving endpoint can't parse will silently break token refresh. Set `headers: { "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" }` and document the expected request/response contract for self-hosters.
